title: Cumulonimbus (thunderhead)
def: A cumulonimbus is a very tall, dense storm cloud with a flat anvil top that produces thunderstorms, lightning, heavy rain, hail, and sometimes tornadoes.
look: towering cauliflower shape that reaches very high
flat, spreading anvil at the top
dark, flat base with rain, hail, or lightning below
use: Treat it as a lightning and downpour warning. Get off ridges, open ground, and water, move to a building or hard-topped vehicle, and expect sudden strong gusts.
not: Do not wait for rain to start before moving; lightning can strike miles ahead of the rain. Do not shelter under lone trees.

title: Cumulus clouds
def: Cumulus are puffy, flat-bottomed clouds with a cotton-ball look that usually mean fair weather unless they grow tall.
look: distinct, rounded puffs with sharp edges
flat bases
small ones scattered in a blue sky
use: Small, scattered cumulus mean fair weather. If they build taller through the day and darken, watch for afternoon showers or storms.
not: Do not assume fair weather if they are towering upward fast; that is a thunderstorm in the making.

title: Stratus clouds and fog
def: Stratus is a flat, gray, featureless layer of low cloud, like fog that has lifted off the ground.
look: uniform gray layer with no shape
very low base, sometimes touching hills
drizzle or mist rather than real rain
use: Expect gloomy, damp, cool conditions with little wind and perhaps drizzle. Visibility is poor, so use care navigating.
not: Do not expect real rain or storms from stratus alone; thicker rain comes from nimbostratus.

title: Nimbostratus
def: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark gray layer that blocks the sun and brings steady rain or snow for hours.
look: dark, even gray sky with no visible sun
steady, continuous rain or snow
ragged lower scud clouds under it
use: Plan for long, soaking rain: set up shelter, keep gear dry, and avoid low spots and dry washes that can flood.
not: Do not expect a quick clearing; it usually lasts until the front passes.

title: Cirrus clouds
def: Cirrus are thin, wispy, white streaks high in the sky made of ice crystals, and they often come before a change in weather.
look: thin white hair-like streaks
very high in a blue sky
hooks or tails, sometimes thickening over hours
use: A few mean fair weather. If they thicken and lower into a sheet over a day, a warm front and rain may follow in about 24 hours.
not: Do not treat a few scattered streaks as a storm warning on their own.

title: Cirrostratus and halo around the sun or moon
def: Cirrostratus is a thin, milky veil of high cloud that makes a ring (halo) around the sun or moon, and it often means rain or snow is coming within a day.
look: bright ring around the sun or moon
thin, milky sheet across the sky
sun or moon still visible through it
use: Expect weather to turn within roughly 12 to 24 hours. Use the time to prepare shelter and gear.
not: Do not treat it as a guarantee; sometimes the front passes by without rain.

title: Altocumulus (mackerel sky)
def: Altocumulus are white or gray patches or rolls of cloud at mid-levels, and in a warm humid morning they can mean afternoon thunderstorms.
look: rows or patches of rounded cloudlets
mid-level, smaller than cumulus
turrets rising from the tops (castellanus) mean unstable air
use: If you see turrets or they appear on a warm, sticky morning, watch for storms by afternoon.
not: Do not mistake them for harmless cirrocumulus; check the size and height of the puffs.

title: Altostratus
also: sun looks like through ground glass
def: Altostratus is a gray or blue-gray mid-level sheet through which the sun appears dimly, like looking through frosted glass.
look: gray sheet with a dim, watery sun
no halo
lowering and thickening over hours
use: It usually thickens ahead of a warm front, so expect steady rain or snow within several hours.
not: Do not expect sharp shadows or a halo; those point to thinner cirrostratus.

title: Stratocumulus
def: Stratocumulus are low, lumpy gray and white clouds in rolls or patches that cover much of the sky, often with little rain.
look: rounded masses joined in rows
gray with brighter gaps
low and common after a front
use: Usually dry or light drizzle at most. Conditions often clear toward evening.
not: Do not expect storms or steady rain from them.

title: Lenticular cloud
def: A lenticular is a smooth, lens-shaped cloud that sits over or downwind of mountains where strong winds flow in waves.
look: smooth lens or stacked-plate shape
stays in one place while air streams through
near mountains with strong wind aloft
use: Treat it as a sign of strong winds aloft and possibly rough air and gusty winds at the summit or downwind. Weather may be changing.
not: Do not mistake it for a normal cloud that will pass; it will stay put as long as the wind blows.

title: Mammatus clouds
def: Mammatus are pouch-like bulges that hang from the underside of a cloud, usually a thunderstorm anvil.
look: lumpy pouches under an anvil
often seen after a storm has passed
dramatic lighting at sunset
use: They mark a strong storm system. Stay alert for severe weather and move to shelter if a storm is still near.
not: Do not take them as a sign that a tornado is coming; they are not a tornado warning.

title: Shelf cloud and gust front
also: wall of cloud ahead of storm
def: A shelf cloud is a low, wedge-shaped wall of cloud on the leading edge of a thunderstorm's cold outflow, with strong straight-line winds right behind it.
look: long horizontal band with a smooth leading edge
dark, ragged cloud behind it
sudden cool breeze and a wind shift before the rain
use: Take shelter now. Damaging gusts, heavy rain, and hail arrive within minutes of the shelf cloud.
not: Do not confuse it with a wall cloud or tornado; it does not rotate, but its winds can still cause damage.

title: Wall cloud and funnel cloud
def: A wall cloud is a localized lowering of the rain-free base of a thunderstorm, and rotation there can lead to a tornado; a funnel cloud is a rotating condensation funnel that has not reached the ground.
look: a lowering that looks like a wall under the storm base
visible rotation or rapid upward motion
a funnel hanging from the base
use: Take shelter immediately in a sturdy building, in an interior room at the lowest level, or in a ditch if there is nothing else. Heed the NWS tornado warning.
not: Do not try to outrun it by driving across open country, and do not shelter under an overpass.

title: Contrails as a sign
def: Contrails are the trails of cloud behind high aircraft; if they stay long and spread, the high air is moist and weather may change.
look: short, quickly vanishing contrails mean dry upper air
long lasting, spreading trails mean moist upper air
trails that merge into thin cirrus sheets
use: Use them as a hint of a coming change, along with other signs like wind shift and falling pressure.
not: Do not use them alone to forecast; they only suggest moisture aloft.

title: Fog: radiation, advection, and valley fog
def: Fog is a cloud at ground level; it forms when air cools to its dew point, most often on calm, clear nights or when moist air moves over a cold surface.
look: radiation or valley fog: calm, clear night, fog in low spots
advection fog: warm moist air moving over cold water or land
fog burns off with morning sun unless it is a thick marine layer
use: Slow down, stay on a known route, use a compass or GPS, and keep a rope or buddy between you if you must move. Expect clearing midday for valley fog.
not: Do not travel by sight alone in dense fog near cliffs, rivers, or roads.

title: Thunderstorm life cycle
def: A thunderstorm grows from rising warm moist air, matures with heavy rain and lightning, and then weakens as downdrafts cut off the updraft.
look: towering cumulus growing fast
anvil top and rain, hail, and lightning at maturity
cold outflow winds that spread out before the rain
use: Watch for fast-growing towers on warm afternoons and plan to be off ridges early. Storms often last 30 minutes to an hour but can repeat along a line.
not: Do not assume the danger ends when the rain stops; lightning can strike up to 10 miles away.

title: Flash-to-bang: counting the distance to lightning
also: how far away is the lightning
def: Count the seconds from a lightning flash to its thunder; every five seconds is about one mile (three seconds is about one kilometer).
look: see the flash, start counting
hear the thunder, stop
divide by five for miles, by three for kilometers
use: If you hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck. Go to safe shelter and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
not: Do not use a long count as a reason to stay out; lightning can strike 10 miles from the storm. Do not count on the same storm cell moving away.

title: Tornado warning signs
also: how to know a tornado is coming
roaring sound like a freight train
def: Tornado signs are a dark, greenish sky, large hail, a rotating wall cloud, a loud roar, and a debris cloud at ground level.
look: dark, green-tinged sky and large hail
rotating, lowering cloud base
loud continuous roar like a freight train
funnel or debris cloud near the ground
use: If a tornado warning is issued or you see these signs, go to shelter now. A tornado watch means conditions are favorable, so stay alert.
not: Do not wait to see the funnel, and do not open windows. Rain wrapped tornadoes can be hidden.

title: Tornado safety
also: what to do in a tornado
def: In a tornado, get to the lowest floor of a sturdy building, in an interior room away from windows, and protect your head and neck.
look: interior room, closet, or bathroom on the lowest floor
basement or storm shelter is best
mobile homes and vehicles are not safe
use: Cover yourself with mattresses or blankets and wear a helmet if you have one. If caught outside with no shelter, lie flat in a ditch or low spot and cover your head.
not: Do not shelter in a mobile home, do not stay in a vehicle if a sturdy building is close, and do not hide under an overpass.

title: Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale
def: The EF scale rates a tornado from EF0 to EF5 by the damage it causes and the wind speeds estimated from it.
look: EF0: 65 to 85 mph, light damage
EF2: 111 to 135 mph, considerable damage
EF4: 166 to 200 mph, devastating damage
EF5: over 200 mph, incredible damage
use: Use it to understand reports after a tornado. The rating is assigned after the damage survey, not in advance.
not: Do not read a rating as a measure of the size or width of the tornado alone.

title: Hurricane categories (Saffir-Simpson)
def: The Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes from category 1 to 5 by sustained wind speed, but flooding and storm surge cause most deaths.
look: category 1: 74 to 95 mph
category 3: 111 to 129 mph, a major hurricane
category 5: 157 mph or higher
use: Prepare early by category and by the local storm surge and rainfall forecasts. Follow evacuation orders for surge zones.
not: Do not judge your risk from the category alone. A weaker storm can flood a large area.

title: Storm surge
def: Storm surge is the rise in sea level pushed ashore by a hurricane's winds, and it is the biggest killer in hurricanes.
look: water rising far above normal high tide
strongest to the right of the storm's track in the north hemisphere
flooding miles inland on low coasts
use: Leave when told to evacuate a surge zone, and go inland or uphill. Plan the route before the storm.
not: Do not stay behind in a surge zone, and do not drive into flooded roads.

title: Hurricane safety
also: what to do in a hurricane
def: Hurricane safety means knowing your evacuation zone, leaving early if told to, and sheltering in a safe interior room if you stay.
look: know your zone and route
supplies for several days: water, food, medicine, radio, power bank
windows covered and outside objects secured
use: Follow official evacuation orders, fill gas, and keep a battery radio. During the storm stay inside, away from windows, in an interior room on a lower floor, but above any flood or surge level.
not: Do not go out in the eye, and do not use candles; use flashlights.

title: Watch, warning, and advisory
also: difference between a watch and a warning
def: A watch means conditions are favorable for the hazard; a warning means it is happening or about to happen; an advisory means it will be a nuisance.
look: watch: be prepared
warning: take action now
advisory: be careful
use: When a warning is issued for your location, act at once. When a watch is issued, review your plan and keep a radio on.
not: Do not wait for a warning to prepare when a watch is in effect.

title: NOAA Weather Radio
def: NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts National Weather Service forecasts and alerts around the clock on seven VHF frequencies.
look: frequencies between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz
a tone alert and SAME code for your county
battery or hand crank radios work in outages
use: Keep a weather radio with fresh batteries, set to your county's SAME code, as a way to get warnings when cell service and power are out.
not: Do not rely only on phone alerts; towers and batteries can fail.

title: Blizzard and winter storm safety
def: A blizzard is a storm with sustained winds or gusts of 35 mph or more and low visibility from falling or blowing snow for at least three hours.
look: falling or blowing snow with very low visibility
strong winds and drifting
dangerous wind chills
use: Stay inside, stay put in a vehicle if stranded (run the engine only briefly with the tailpipe clear), and keep warm and hydrated. Use layers, a hat, and bright markers.
not: Do not leave a stranded car to walk in a whiteout unless safety is in sight, and do not let the tailpipe get blocked by snow.

title: Freezing rain and ice storms
def: Freezing rain falls as liquid and freezes on contact, coating everything with ice; it is far more damaging than sleet.
look: glazed trees, wires, and roads
sleet bounces and rattles, freezing rain coats and sticks
limbs and lines breaking under the weight
use: Stay off roads, stay clear of trees and power lines, and prepare for outages. Keep warm and do not use generators indoors.
not: Do not walk or drive on a glazed surface, and do not go near downed lines.

title: Wind chill
def: Wind chill is how cold the air feels on bare skin because wind carries away body heat; it affects people and animals, not objects.
look: a stronger wind makes the same temperature feel colder
at around minus 20 F (minus 29 C) wind chill, frostbite can occur in about 30 minutes
at minus 40 and lower it is much faster
use: Dress for the wind chill: windproof outer layer, covered skin, and warm insulation, and check for frostbite on exposed skin.
not: Do not think the wind chill lowers the actual air temperature or freezes water faster.

title: Heat index
def: The heat index combines air temperature and humidity to show how hot it really feels, because sweat cannot cool you when the air is humid.
look: high humidity makes it feel hotter
heat index above 103 F (39 C) is dangerous
full sun can add up to 15 F
use: Do hard work in the early morning or evening, rest in the shade, and drink water. Check on older people, children, and pets.
not: Do not rely on the air temperature alone, and do not leave anyone in a parked car.

title: Dew point and humidity
def: The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and dew or fog forms; a higher dew point means muggier air.
look: dew point under 10 C (50 F): dry, comfortable
above 18 C (65 F): sticky
air temperature falling toward the dew point means dew or fog
use: If the night temperature will fall to the dew point, expect dew or fog and condensation on gear. Put gear in a tent or bag to keep it dry.
not: Do not confuse dew point with relative humidity; the dew point tells you how much moisture is in the air.

title: Reading the barometer trend
def: A barometer measures air pressure; how it changes over a few hours tells more than the number itself.
look: falling slowly: clouds and weather deteriorating
falling fast: a storm is near
rising: clearing and drier air
steady: little change
use: Note the pressure every few hours. A fast fall, such as 3 hPa or more in three hours, calls for preparing for rough weather. Watch altimeter drift as a pressure change.
not: Do not trust a single reading; use the trend. Do not mistake pressure change from altitude for weather.

title: Cold front
def: A cold front is the leading edge of a cooler air mass that pushes under warmer air, causing a narrow band of storms, a wind shift, and a drop in temperature.
look: a line of towering clouds and showers or storms
wind shifts to the west or northwest in the northern hemisphere
pressure falls then rises and temperature drops sharply
use: Expect a brief, sometimes severe band of weather followed by clearing and cooler, drier air. Secure camp before it arrives.
not: Do not expect a long soak; the front is usually fast, though it can be fierce.

title: Warm front
also: steady rain ahead of warm air
def: A warm front is where warm air slides over cooler air, bringing a long period of thickening clouds and steady rain or snow, then milder weather.
look: cirrus, then cirrostratus, then altostratus, then nimbostratus
pressure falls steadily
winds back to the south or southeast before the front
use: Expect a day or so of build-up, then hours of steady precipitation and warmer, muggier air after it passes.
not: Do not expect sharp storms; the weather is usually steady rather than violent.

title: Wind shifts and Buys Ballot's law
also: which way is the low pressure
def: Wind shifts show a passing front: in the northern hemisphere, stand with your back to the wind and the low pressure is on your left.
look: wind backing (counterclockwise) with falling pressure ahead of a low
sudden shift to the northwest with a cold front
calm followed by gusts
use: Use wind direction with cloud and pressure changes to judge where the weather is coming from, and plan for a front when the wind swings.
not: Do not use the rule in the southern hemisphere without reversing it, and do not use it for local mountain winds.

title: Beaufort wind scale
def: The Beaufort scale describes wind force from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane) using what you can see.
look: force 4: moderate breeze, dust and small branches move (11-16 knots)
force 6: strong breeze, large branches sway, umbrellas hard to use (22-27 knots)
force 8: gale, twigs break off trees, walking is hard (34-40 knots)
force 12: hurricane force, 64 knots or more
use: Use it to judge conditions and decide to stay off the water, ridgelines, and exposed trails at force 6 and above.
not: Do not take the word choice as an exact speed; it is an observed estimate.

title: Mountain weather
def: Mountain weather changes fast: temperatures fall with height, winds strengthen, and storms often build by early afternoon.
look: temperature drops about 6.5 C per 1,000 m (3.5 F per 1,000 ft)
afternoon cumulus towers in summer
strong winds on exposed ridges and cols
use: Start early, be off summits and ridges by noon, and turn back when clouds build. Carry rain and warm layers even on fair days.
not: Do not push on to the summit when storms are building, and do not assume the weather in the valley matches the summit.

title: Microburst and downburst
def: A microburst is a small, intense downdraft from a thunderstorm that spreads out at the ground and can knock down trees in one direction.
look: sudden strong wind at the leading edge of a storm
dust or rain streaking down
trees down in a one-directional pattern afterward
use: Move away from trees and into a sturdy shelter at the first sign of a strong, sudden gust ahead of a storm.
not: Do not camp under tall dead trees or rely on a tent in a thunderstorm.

title: Flash flood risk
def: A flash flood is a rapid rise of water, often from storms miles upstream, and it can reach you under a clear sky.
look: heavy rain upstream, rising and muddy creeks
a rumbling roar in a canyon, or debris in the water
low-water crossings and dry washes
use: Move to high ground at once, avoid canyons and washes in storm season, and never drive or walk through floodwater. Turn around, don't drown.
not: Do not cross moving water. As little as 6 inches (15 cm) can knock you down and about a foot (30 cm) can float a car.

title: Wildfire smoke and air quality
def: Wildfire smoke contains fine particles that can harm the lungs and heart; the air quality index (AQI) shows when to limit time outside.
look: AQI above 100 is unhealthy for sensitive groups
above 150 is unhealthy for all
haze, ash, and a smell of smoke
use: Stay indoors with windows closed, run a HEPA filter, and use a well-fitted N95 respirator outside if you must. Limit exertion.
not: Do not rely on a cloth or paper mask for smoke, and do not exercise hard outdoors on smoky days.

title: Wildfire evacuation
def: For a wildfire, leave early when told to or when smoke and flames are near; waiting is the biggest mistake.
look: official evacuation order or warning
smoke, ember showers, and a wind shift toward you
roads clogging up
use: Take people, pets, medicines, papers, and a go bag, close windows and doors, and follow known evacuation routes. Tell someone where you are going.
not: Do not wait for flames to be in view, and do not try to defend a home against a major fire if told to leave.

title: Dust storm (haboob)
def: A haboob is a wall of dust pushed ahead of a thunderstorm's outflow, dropping visibility to near zero within seconds.
look: a towering brown wall approaching
sudden strong gusts and a drop in visibility
dry air and dust over deserts
use: Pull off the road as far as you can, turn off lights, set the parking brake, and keep your foot off the brake pedal. Cover your nose and mouth.
not: Do not keep driving in a dust storm or leave lights on in a parked vehicle; others may follow them.

title: Temperature inversion and cold air pooling
also: cold in the valley at night
def: On calm clear nights, cold air sinks and pools in valleys while the slopes above stay warmer; this is a temperature inversion.
look: smoke or fog layers lie flat
valley floors much colder than the slopes
still, clear night
use: Camp on the slope or bench, not the valley floor. Frost and fog form in the low spots first.
not: Do not pitch camp in the lowest spot to hide from wind; it will be the coldest.

title: Folk weather signs: what holds up
def: Some old sayings work because they match real changes in air pressure and moisture; others are myths.
look: red sky at night, shepherd's delight: often works in mid-latitudes where weather moves west to east
a ring around the moon: thin high cloud ahead of a front
smoke that hangs low or rises slowly: low pressure and humid air
swallows and bats flying low: insects stay low in humid air
use: Treat folk signs as clues to combine with cloud types, wind shift, and pressure. If several agree, expect a change.
not: Do not trust a single saying, and do not rely on animal behavior as the only forecast.

title: Lightning myths
also: if the sky is clear lightning cannot hit
def: Lightning can strike the same place many times, can reach 10 miles from a storm, and rubber tires do not protect you; a hard-topped metal vehicle does.
look: bolts from the blue strike under clear skies near a storm
tall isolated objects are struck repeatedly
a car protects because of its metal body, not its tires
use: When thunder is heard, go inside a substantial building or a hard-topped vehicle and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
not: Do not shelter under a tree, in a tent, in a shed, or in an open-sided shelter. Do not stay on the water.

title: Power outage basics in a storm
def: In a storm outage, keep warm, use flashlights, keep fridge and freezer doors closed, and run generators outside, far from the house.
look: flashlights and battery lantern, not candles
closed fridge keeps food safe about four hours, a full freezer about 48 hours
a battery radio for alerts
use: Use dry ice or ice for the fridge, and eat perishables first. Unplug sensitive electronics, and leave one light on to know when power returns.
not: Do not use a gas oven or grill for heat, and do not run a generator in a garage or near a window.
